t: What a Smart Home Hub Actually Is
e: Today Apple's HomeView goes on sale in the US, and it can act as a home hub. But what is a hub, and why does it matter more than the screen?
b:
Today, Apple's HomeView goes on sale in the US and a handful of other countries. Among other things, it can act as the hub for an Apple home. That sounds technical, and most people nod politely and move on. But the hub is the most important part of any smart home, much more important than the screen on the counter.
So: what is it?

The screen is the window, the hub is the engine
A display shows you your home and lets you tap a button. A hub is the device that actually does the work, all day and all night, whether anyone is looking or not:

It knows every device: lights, sensors, blinds, radiators, the lock.
It runs the automations: "if the window opens, turn the radiator down", "half an hour before sunset, switch on the lamp".
It remembers: temperatures, energy use, when the door was opened.
It talks every language the devices speak.

Without a hub, every device is on its own, with its own app. With a hub, they work together as one home. That's what I mean by a system, as opposed to a collection of gadgets.
Many homes have several hubs without knowing it
If you have smart lights from one brand, a heating system from another and a voice speaker from a third, you probably have three hubs already: a bridge for the lights, a box for the heating, and the speaker, which often doubles as a hub. Each one does its own thing, and they barely talk to each other. That's exactly the problem I described in my post on vendor lock-in.
The languages devices speak
Devices talk to the hub by radio, and there are a few common "languages":

Wi-Fi, which most people know, works for many devices but isn't ideal for small battery sensors.
Zigbee, a low-power mesh network, is widely used for sensors, switches and lights.
Thread is newer and carries the Matter standard, which many big manufacturers now support.
Z-Wave is another established standard, common in some regions.

A good hub speaks several of these. For radios it doesn't have built in, a small USB stick is added, for example the Home Assistant Connect ZBT-2, which handles Zigbee or Thread.

Where the brain lives matters most
The most important question about any hub is where its thinking happens. Some hubs are mainly a relay to the manufacturer's servers: if the internet or the company's service goes down, so does your home. Others work locally: the automations run in the box in your hallway, and the internet is only needed for things like remote access or weather data.

t: Voice Control in Swiss German: An Honest Progress Report
e: 'Mach s Liecht im Wohnzimmer aa.' Can a smart home understand that, without sending your voice to the cloud? Where things stand today.
b:
"Mach s Liecht im Wohnzimmer aa." For most people in German-speaking Switzerland, that's simply how you'd say it. Not "Schalte das Licht im Wohnzimmer ein". The question is whether a smart home understands it, and whether it can do so without sending every word to a server somewhere.
Here is where things honestly stand, as of November 2026.

Why Swiss German is hard for machines
Swiss German is spoken, not written. There is no standard spelling, every region sounds different, and "Chuchichäschtli" is not in anyone's dictionary. A speech recogniser therefore has to do two things at once: understand the dialect, and write it down as Standard German text that the system can act on. That's a translation task as much as a listening one.
The numbers show how hard that is. According to a Swiss AI company that published a fine-tuned model in May 2026, the well-known open speech recogniser Whisper gets roughly one word in four wrong when it hears Swiss German without special training (about 26% word error rate). Their model, trained on recordings from the Swiss parliament, roughly halves that, to about 13%. But they say themselves that it works best on formal speech and worse on spontaneous everyday speech, noisy rooms, and dialects other than Bernese.
What works today, locally
Home Assistant can process voice entirely on your own hardware, with no recordings leaving the house. It offers two ways of turning speech into text:

Speech-to-Phrase only understands a fixed set of home commands, but it's very fast: under a second, even on a small Home Assistant Green.
Whisper tries to understand everything, but needs much more computing power. On a small computer like a Raspberry Pi 4 an answer takes about eight seconds; on a faster mini-PC it's under a second.

Home Assistant's own documentation adds an honest warning: quality varies a lot from language to language, so check how it works in yours.
In practice, that means today:

Short commands work well, especially when spoken somewhat towards Standard German: "Licht Wohnzimmer aus", "Storen runter", "Wie warm ist es im Schlafzimmer?"
Free dialect is still hit and miss. A long sentence in broad Zürichdeutsch or Walliserdeutsch is not yet reliably understood by a local system.
The answer comes back in Standard German, spoken by a local voice.

t: Airing, Heating and Mould
e: Every winter the same question: how often should you air, and how warm should it be? A few sensors take the guessing out of it.
b:
It starts small. A grey shadow in the corner behind the wardrobe. Black dots on the silicone in the shower. Windows that are wet on the inside every morning. Then come the questions: am I airing wrong? Is it the building? And who pays?

Where the moisture comes from
People produce a lot of water just by living. According to a brochure by the Federal Office of Public Health (BAG), a household of four releases about 7.5 litres of water vapour into the air every day, up to 12 litres with a lot of showering, cooking and drying laundry. That moisture has to go somewhere. If it can't get out, it settles where the wall is coldest: in corners, on outside walls, behind furniture.
Older buildings without wall insulation and ground-floor flats are more at risk, the BAG notes.
What the guidelines say

Humidity: the BAG recommends 30 to 50% relative humidity indoors. On very cold days it shouldn't go above 40%, and in the heating season not above 50%.
Airing: a guidance sheet from the canton of Basel-Stadt, based on the BAG, recommends airing with the windows wide open at least three times a day for 10 minutes, ideally with a through-draught.
Heating: about 21 degrees in living rooms. In well-insulated buildings, bedrooms can be cooler.
Furniture: keep at least 10 cm between large furniture and outside walls, so air can circulate.

All of this is easy to read and hard to keep up every day. Who knows what the humidity in the bedroom is right now?
What a few sensors change

Humidity you can see. Small sensors in the bedroom, the bathroom and behind the wardrobe on the outside wall show the real values. You no longer have to guess.
A reminder at the right moment. When the humidity climbs above the limit you've set, a lamp changes colour or your phone gets a short note: time to air.
And a reminder to close again. After ten minutes, the next note: the room is aired, close the window so it doesn't cool down.
Heating that pauses. A sensor on the window turns the radiator down while it's open. Airing then doesn't waste heat, as described in my post on saving energy.
The bathroom after showering. The fan runs until the humidity is back to normal, or a dehumidifier on a smart plug switches on by itself.

For renters: a record helps
If mould does appear in a rented flat, the question of fault often comes up quickly. A sensor log of how you heated and aired is much better than "I always aired properly". In my post for renters I describe why such records are useful.

t: A Home That Remembers for You
e: Keys, the stove, the appointment at three: with ADHD, the hard part is often remembering at the right moment. A home can help by putting the reminder where it's needed.
b:
You're already at the tram stop when the thought arrives: did I switch off the stove? You go back. It was off. Tomorrow it'll be the keys, the day after the appointment you were sure you'd remember.
For many adults with ADHD, this isn't occasional. It's daily life. And it has very little to do with not trying hard enough.

A note first: I'm not a doctor, and this post is not medical advice. If you think ADHD might affect you, a qualified clinician is the right first step.
Forgetting is part of the picture
The official diagnostic criteria for ADHD literally include "often loses things", with keys, wallets and mobile phones as examples, and "is often forgetful in daily activities", like chores, errands, paying bills and keeping appointments. Depending on the definition, studies estimate that between about 1 in 40 and 1 in 15 adults worldwide are affected.
In adults, the visible restlessness of childhood often turns inward. What stays is the difficulty of remembering to do something at the right moment, judging time and starting tasks.
What helps, according to research
The best-supported approach is not "trying harder" and not brain-training apps. Training apps improve scores in the app, but studies show the effect doesn't carry over into daily life.
What does help is structure outside your head: calendars, task lists, breaking big jobs into small steps, and reminders placed exactly where and when the action happens. Psychologists call this the "point of performance". The reminder to take the keys belongs at the door, not in a notebook.
That's where a home can help. I want to be honest, though: there are no studies yet on smart homes for ADHD. What follows is applying a well-supported principle, cues in the right place, with today's technology. It's not a proven treatment.
Reminders where you need them

At the front door. When you leave, a small light by the door turns amber if a window is still open or the iron is still on. One glance, before the door closes.
The stove question. An iron or a kettle on a smart plug can be checked from your phone, or switched off automatically after a while. For the stove itself, an electrician can fit a stove guard that switches it off if it's left on.
Time you can see. Ten minutes before you need to leave for an appointment, the hallway light changes colour. Time becomes visible instead of something you have to keep track of in your head.

t: Living at Home With Dementia: Help Without Surveillance
e: Most people with dementia in Switzerland live at home, cared for by family. A few quiet helpers can make that safer, if they respect the person they're meant to protect.
b:
Every evening at seven, the daughter calls. "Did you eat? Is the stove off? Did you lock the door?" Her mother answers patiently, then less patiently. She doesn't like being checked on. Her daughter doesn't like having to check. Both of them would rather just talk.
Many families in Switzerland know this call.

Most people with dementia live at home
According to the Federal Office of Public Health (BAG), around 166,300 people in Switzerland live with dementia, and about 35,800 are newly diagnosed each year. By far the largest share of them live at home, supported by partners, children, neighbours and Spitex.
Living at home for as long as possible is what most people want. It also means that the people around them carry a lot of worry: the stove, the night, the front door, a fall that nobody notices.
Where a home can quietly help
In the early stage of dementia, a few well-chosen helpers can take some of that worry away, without changing how the home looks or feels.

A stove guard. A small device fitted to an electric stove by an electrician. It notices overheating, smoke or a pot left on for too long, and switches the stove off with a warning tone. It's meant for the early stage, when cooking is still part of daily life.
Soft light at night. Motion sensors switch on a gentle light on the way to the bathroom, so nobody has to search for a switch in the dark. I wrote about this in Darker Evenings, Safer Hallways.
The front door at night. If the door opens between midnight and six, the hallway light comes on and a family member gets a short message. Nobody is locked in, and nobody is woken for nothing during the day.
Water. A leak sensor under the sink and the washing machine notices a running tap or an overflowing basin early.
A quiet daily sign of life. If there's been no movement in the flat by mid-morning, the daughter gets a message. On every other day she knows, without asking, that the morning has started as usual. The evening call can go back to being a conversation.

For emergencies, use what's built for emergencies
Konihaus is not an emergency service, and a smart home shouldn't pretend to be one. If someone needs to reach help at any time, Switzerland has monitored emergency call services, for example from the Swiss Red Cross, with a control centre that answers around the clock. A smart home can complement them, never replace them.

t: Electricity Gets a Little Cheaper in 2027. It's Still Expensive.
e: A typical Swiss household pays about CHF 53 less for electricity in 2027. Where the real savings are, and why I won't promise you a percentage.
b:
In September, the Federal Electricity Commission (ElCom) published next year's tariffs. The headline: electricity gets cheaper. The small print: not by much, and not everywhere.

Electricity prices 2027 in Switzerland: the numbers
For a typical household using 4,500 kWh a year, the median price in 2027 is 26.5 centimes per kWh, about 4% less than this year. Over a year, that's a bill of around CHF 1,194, or CHF 53 less than in 2026.
Behind the average, two things move in opposite directions. The energy itself gets cheaper (about 6% less), while the grid part gets slightly more expensive (about 2% more). ElCom itself says prices are stabilising "at a still quite high level".
And the average hides big differences. Some suppliers cut their prices by a quarter. Others go up: one municipality in Aargau pays almost 38 centimes per kWh in 2027. What you pay depends on where you live. You can look up your own municipality on ElCom's comparison site, strompreis.elcom.admin.ch.
What CHF 53 means
CHF 53 a year is a nice dinner. It's welcome, but it doesn't change much. If you want your electricity bill to really go down, the lever isn't the tariff. It's how much you use, and when.
Where the electricity goes
Most of us have no idea which devices use how much. Some numbers help:

Stand-by. According to the Swiss Agency for Efficient Energy Use (S.A.F.E.), stand-by accounts for about 10% of electricity use in an average household. For the typical household above, that would be around 450 kWh, or roughly CHF 120 a year at the 2027 median price (my calculation). The TV that's never quite off, the printer, the game console, the old stereo.
The forgotten appliances. The second freezer in the cellar. The fridge from 2004. The dehumidifier nobody switched off in spring.
Heating and hot water, if they run on electricity: an electric boiler, old electric heaters, a heat pump. In those homes, heating is usually by far the biggest item.

What a smart home can do, honestly
It makes it visible. An energy dashboard, like the one in the Konihaus app, shows what runs when. Many people are surprised the first week: the house uses electricity at three in the morning, when everybody is asleep. Once you can see it, you can decide.
It switches off what nobody needs. A smart plug can cut the TV corner or the home office completely at night. One thing to be honest about: a smart plug uses a little electricity itself. So it belongs where it saves more than it costs, at the media cor

t: Smart Home as a Renter: What You Can Do Without Asking
e: Most Swiss households rent. A smart home is still possible, if it plugs in, screws in or sticks on, and comes out again when you move.
b:
"I'd love a smart home, but I'm renting." I hear that sentence more than any other. Behind it is a reasonable worry: you don't want trouble with the landlord, and you don't want to leave your deposit on the wall when you move out.
The good news: most of what makes a home smarter doesn't touch the building at all.

What the law says, in short
In Switzerland, changes to a rented flat need the landlord's written consent. That's Article 260a of the Code of Obligations. Small things are a different matter: holes for pictures or a shelf are generally accepted without asking. But even then, the landlord can ask you to restore the original condition when you leave, for example to fill the holes properly.
That's the frame. What it means in practice depends on your lease, so read it, and if in doubt, ask in writing. I'm not a lawyer, and this isn't legal advice.
Smart home for renters: the simple rule
If it plugs in, screws into a lamp, sits on a shelf or sticks on, and leaves nothing behind when you take it away, you're generally on the safe side. That covers more than you'd think:

Smart plugs for lamps, the coffee machine, the fan in summer.
Smart bulbs in the lamps you already have.
Battery sensors for doors, windows, motion, temperature, humidity and water, mounted with removable adhesive strips.
The hub, a small box on a shelf next to the router.
Radiator thermostats. In most flats you can swap the thermostat head on the valve without tools. Keep the original head and put it back when you move.
Lights under cabinets or the bed on a plug, without wiring, for example as a night light on the way to the bathroom.

Ask first
Some things touch the building, the shared areas or other people. Ask your landlord, or the administration, in writing before you do them:

Anything wired into 230 volts: switches, ceiling lights, the fuse box. That's for an electrician anyway.
Motors for exterior blinds (Storen). They belong to the building. Many wired blinds can still be made smart without new wiring: if the motor cable has a plug connector, a plug-in radio receiver, for example from Somfy for roller shutters or exterior venetian blinds, goes between the motor and the power supply and can be removed again later. It still sits on the building's 230-volt installation, so ask first and have it fitted by a specialist.
The front door cylinder or a lock on it, especially if it's part of a building-wide key system.

t: Darker Evenings, Safer Hallways
e: Most falls at home don't happen on a mountain path, they happen on the way to the bathroom. Soft light that switches on by itself is one of the simplest things a home can do.
b:
It's three in the morning. You wake up and need the bathroom. The switch is on the other side of the room. The ceiling light would be blinding, and it might wake your partner. So you get up in the dark, feel your way along the wall, and hope the slippers aren't where you left them.
Everybody knows this walk. Most of us have done it a thousand times without thinking. But it's exactly the kind of moment where things go wrong.

Fall prevention starts at home
According to the Swiss Council for Accident Prevention (BFU), around 127,000 people in Switzerland are injured in falls at home every year. That's about one in eight of all accidents outside work. Some of these injuries take a long time to heal, and with age, a fall can cost a piece of independence.
The BFU names poor lighting as one of the risk factors. It's not the only one. Loose rugs, missing handrails, medication and balance all play a part. But light is the one a home can take care of by itself.
Night lights that come on before you do
The idea is simple. Small motion sensors notice when you get up at night. A soft light switches on, along the way you actually walk: beside the bed, in the hallway, in the bathroom.

At night it's gentle: low brightness, warm colour, enough to see the edge of the door frame but not enough to wake you fully, or anyone else.
During the day it's normal: the same lights work at full brightness, or not at all if there's daylight.
It switches itself off a few minutes after you're back in bed.
No switch to find. That's the whole point.

Technically this is a few battery sensors and either smart bulbs in the lamps you already have, or a thin LED strip under the bed. No drilling needed, which also makes it work in a rented flat.

A second layer, if you want it
For some people, light is enough. Others, especially those who live alone, or their families, want a little more:

An alarm button by the bed or in the bathroom. One press sends a message to the people you've chosen: a daughter, a neighbour, a friend.
A quiet morning check. If there's been no movement in the flat by a time you set, someone you trust gets a short message to give you a call.

To be clear about what this is: Konihaus is not an emergency service. The messages go to the people you name, not to a control centre, and I don't call the ambulance myself. And no system can promise that nothing happens. What it can do is make a fall less likely in the first place, and make it less likely that one goes unnoticed.

t: Frost Watch for the Holiday Home
e: A frozen pipe in an empty holiday home is often only noticed when the ice melts. A few sensors let you know while there's still time to act.
b:
The last autumn weekend in the mountains is over. You close the shutters, turn the heating down, lock the door and drive home. The next visit is planned for the ski holidays in February.
In between, there are weeks when nobody is there. And somewhere in January, a cold night comes that is a few degrees colder than the house was built for.

The damage you don't see
When water freezes in a pipe, it expands, and the pipe can burst. The tricky part, as Swiss insurers point out: you often don't notice when it happens. The pipe is plugged with ice. Only when it thaws does the water start running, sometimes for days, through an empty flat, into the walls and into the flat below.
Why "frost protection" on the radiator isn't enough
Many people turn the radiator valve to the snowflake symbol and feel safe. AXA explains why that's not enough: the frost setting protects the radiator, not the pipes. Their advice is never to switch the heating off completely and to keep it at least on level 1.
The real risk sits where the thermostat isn't. A pipe in an outside wall. The bathroom on the north side. The utility room, the garage, the spot where the water main comes into the house. The living room can be at a comfortable 10 degrees while the pipe behind the bathroom wall is at zero.
Frost protection with a few sensors
You can't be in the mountains and in Zurich at the same time. But your home can tell you how it's doing:

Temperature sensors in the coldest spots, not the living room. If the bathroom drops below 5 degrees, you get a message while there's still time to act.
Leak sensors under the boiler, the washing machine and the kitchen sink. If water appears, you know within seconds, not at the next visit.
Heating you can check from home. See the temperature in every room, and raise it by a few degrees before a cold snap.
A warm house when you arrive. The heating starts in good time before you come, as described in my post on energy.
A short weekly note: everything's fine. Often that's the most valuable message of all.

If you want to go one step further, a plumber can fit a motorised main valve that closes the water automatically when a leak sensor raises the alarm. That's building work, so it's one for owners, not tenants.
Who goes there when the alert comes?
A message on your phone helps only if someone can act on it. So before winter, it's worth agreeing on one thing: who has a key and can go and look? A neighbour, the caretaker, someone from the village.

t: Smart Lights: Bulbs, Strips and Lamps, and What You Can Buy in Switzerland
e: The first smart device for most homes is a light. Which bulbs, strips and lamps are worth it, where to buy them in Switzerland, and how to use them for movies, moods and holidays.
b:
Almost every smart home starts with a light. It is cheap, it is visible, and the result is instant: you say "movie time" and the room changes. It is also the first device people get wrong, by buying something that works only with one app, or only with one shop's hub.
This is the first post in a new series. From today there is a new technical post every other day. In this series I'll go through one group of devices at a time: lights, then shades, sensors, heating and more. Each post asks the same questions: what does it do for you, what should you check before buying, and where are the honest limits. And because you asked for it: yes, I'll name brands and say what you can actually buy in Switzerland.

Three kinds of smart light
Bulbs are the easiest start. You replace the bulb, and the lamp you already own becomes smart. The common formats are:

E27, the standard screw base, for most ceiling and floor lamps
E14, the small screw base, for candle-style bulbs in chandeliers and wall lights
GU10, the spotlight with two pins, for ceiling spots and track lighting
GU5.3, the low-voltage spot, found in older halogen installs

Check the base and the shape before you buy, and check whether the lamp is dimmable-rated or enclosed, because heat matters in tight fittings.
LED strips go behind the TV, under a kitchen cabinet, along a shelf or the back of a desk. They give indirect light and the most dramatic colour effects. Look for strips you can cut, with a clear note on length and power supply.
Smart lamps have the light built in. A desk lamp with a warm-to-cool white range, a table lamp that works as a glowing accent, a floor lamp that washes a wall with colour. They are the easiest choice for renters: plug in, done, and the lamp moves with you.

What's on sale in Switzerland
Here is what I found today, 27 October 2026. Prices change, so treat them as a guide.
Hornbach has a clear smart-lamp section. Philips Hue is the most visible brand, with starter sets and the bridge. Hornbach also lists other labels such as EGLO and TINT, and many items carry a "compatible with SMART HOME by hornbach" label. Simple smart white bulbs start at around CHF 8 to 15. Typical bulbs are CHF 15 to 60. Hue colour spots and candles sit higher. A Hue Bridge Pro starter set was listed at CHF 142.95.
IKEA has the broadest and cheapest range in one place. The KAJPLATS bulbs (E27, E14, GU10) cost CHF 7.95 to 14.95, and a starter set with a remote was around CHF 12.95. The SKY

t: Apple HomeView: Why It Isn't Coming Here, and What That Tells Us
e: Apple's new smart display goes on sale in the US and the UK in November, but not in the EU, and there's no date for Switzerland. A calm look at why, and what it means for your home.
b:
On 13 October, Apple announced HomeView: a 7-inch screen on a small speaker base, made for the kitchen counter, the bedside table or, in a second version, the wall. It shows your calendar, plays music, makes FaceTime calls and walks you through a recipe step by step, with timers you start by voice. It controls lights, heating and door locks, shows up to nine camera feeds at once and recognises up to six people in a household, each with their own home screen. It works with Matter devices and can act as the hub for an Apple home on its own.
It costs 299 dollars in the US and 299 pounds in the UK, and goes on sale on 13 November in a first group of countries: the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, India and New Zealand.
It's a beautiful device. And for now, you can't buy it here.

Why HomeView isn't available in Switzerland
Apple built HomeView around Siri AI, its new assistant. Siri AI isn't available on iPhones in the EU, so Apple says HomeView is "not available for sale in the European Union" for now, and that it's working with the EU on a way forward. According to 9to5Mac, this has to do with the EU's Digital Markets Act, which treats the iPhone's operating system differently from Apple's other platforms.
Switzerland isn't in the EU, but it isn't on the launch list either, and no Swiss date has been announced. Siri AI also speaks only English for now. Apple hasn't announced German, French or Italian, the languages most of us actually speak at home here.
What it tells us
This isn't a story about Apple being bad. It's a story about where a device's features come from.
Many of HomeView's features don't live in the device on your counter. They depend on things outside your home: an account, a cloud service, a compatible iPhone (the full feature set needs one that supports Apple Intelligence), sometimes a subscription (some camera features need iCloud+), and decisions made by a company and by regulators far away. When any of those changes, your device changes, even though nothing in your living room did. More on this in Will It Still Work in Ten Years?.
For a speaker, that's an inconvenience. For the thing that switches your heating or unlocks your front door, it's a question worth asking before you buy.
One screen for the whole family. Do we need that?
HomeView's most interesting idea is that one screen serves the whole household. It recognises up to six people by face and voice. When you step up to it, it switches from the shared household view to your

t: The Clocks Go Back Tonight. Your Home Won't Notice.
e: On Sunday the clocks go back an hour. Timers fall behind, but a home that follows the sun just carries on.
b:
Tonight at three in the morning, the clocks in Switzerland go back to two. We get an hour of sleep back, and on Sunday evening it gets dark an hour earlier than the day before.
Most of us know the ritual that follows. The oven clock, the car, the radio alarm in the guest room. And the one we forget: the timer plug that switches the living-room lamp on at six. Either it's now an hour off, or you reset it and the lamp comes on at six again, long after the sun set at a quarter past five.

Timers know the time. They don't know the light.
A timer answers one question: what time is it? The question you actually care about is a different one: is it getting dark?
In June, those two answers are hours apart. By December, the sun sets in Zurich before half past four. A timer set in summer is wrong for most of the year. The clock change only makes it obvious.

A smart home that follows the sun
A smart home can ask the better question. Home Assistant knows where your home is and calculates sunrise and sunset for every day of the year. So instead of "lamp on at 18:00", the rule becomes "lamp on half an hour before sunset". On Saturday that's around ten to six. On Sunday it's around a quarter to five. Nobody has to touch anything.
The same idea works for:

Blinds that close at dusk, so the warmth stays inside and nobody can look into a lit living room.
The entrance light that comes on when it's dark and someone arrives, not at a fixed hour.
The night light in the hallway that only lights up at night, softly, on the way to the bathroom.
Grey November afternoons. With a small brightness sensor, the light comes on when the room is actually dim, even at three o'clock.

And the things that should follow the clock, like the morning heating schedule or a reminder at eight, simply move with the new local time. You don't reset them. The system does that.
Smart doesn't mean everything runs by itself
Not everyone wants the blinds to move on their own. Some people like closing them in the evening; it's part of ending the day. That's fine. The sunset rule can be a gentle reminder instead of an action. Or it only runs when you're away, so the home looks lived-in while you're not there. You decide where the line is.
Why such a small thing matters
The clock change is a small thing. But it shows the difference between a gadget and a system.
A gadget does exactly what you told it once. A system takes the situation into account: daylight, season, whether anyone is home.

t: What does a smart home cost in Switzerland? The honest answer
e: What does a smart home cost in Switzerland? What providers publish, what is missing, and what it costs if you only know you'd like your home to be easier.
b:
In short: A classic smart home with a wired electrical installation costs roughly CHF 3,400 to 16,200 as a one-off, according to published prices in Switzerland. One provider of an open retrofit system charges CHF 4,000 to 7,500 one-off. And there is a variant that starts from CHF 39 a month and is looked after for you. Which one fits depends less on budget than on one question: do you already know what you want?

t: The Pain Points We Stopped Noticing
e: Some chores are so familiar that we no longer see them as chores. A smart home starts with noticing them again.
b:
Hardly anyone enjoys stacking firewood. Some people do love chopping it: the rhythm, the smell, the way the head goes quiet. But then comes the rest. Collecting the pieces, stacking them in order, sweeping up the bark and splinters. That part is boring, so most of us simply buy the wood already chopped, in packs.
I think about this a lot, because it's exactly how I look at the smart home.

Every job has a part nobody misses
Cooking is the same. Plenty of people love it. But hardly anyone does what happens before the kitchen anymore. We buy the chicken ready to cook, sometimes even already cut. The cooking stays ours. The unpleasant part went to someone else long ago, and nobody calls that cheating.
So this was never black and white. Every job has parts we enjoy and parts we only put up with because they come with it.
We get used to everything
The trouble with small annoyances is that they stop feeling like annoyances:

The stove you checked twice before leaving.
The door you walked back to, just to be sure.
The light in a room nobody is in.

These manual routines have been part of life for so long that they no longer register as pain points. They're just how things are.
What has changed is that more and more devices are already IoT-capable, and most of the others can be extended with a sensor or a smart socket. That makes it worth looking again. My approach starts there: not with a shopping list, but with pain-point discovery. What do you do every day that you've simply stopped noticing?

Smart doesn't mean automatic
Smart doesn't mean everything runs by itself. It means the one piece that needs help gets help.
I always switch off the iron after ironing, by hand. I like that: "I switched it off, so it's off" is a real kind of certainty. But once I'm out of the house, a small voice asks: did I? Since the iron sits on a smart socket, I can look. One glance and the question is gone. Nothing was automated. I just got peace of mind.
Doing it manually remains a perfectly good option. The smart layer is there for the moments when you're not sure.

"And what's left for me?"
A fair question: if machines take over everything, what do I do? Nothing says they have to. If you enjoy chopping wood because it switches your head off, keep chopping. Automate the sweeping, or just the part where you wonder whether you switched something off. You decide where the line runs, and it's allowed to move.

t: Swiss Quality: Built in Switzerland, Made to Last
e: From the fuse box to cantonal regulations: we know Swiss homes and stand behind our work for the long run.
b:
More Than a Flag
The Swiss flag is easy to put on a logo. It is much harder to earn.
For us, it is not decoration. It is a promise about how Konihaus is built, where it is run, and how long it is meant to last. Konihaus was founded in a small town near Zurich called Affoltern am Albis, and it is established, maintained, and operated in Switzerland. It is not meant to be a foreign service with a Swiss label on top.

One System, Endless Possibilities
Everyone has seen this: one outlet, one adapter, then another adapter on top of it, and another, until the wall looks like a sculpture. Every new device makes it worse. It works, until it doesn't, and then nobody knows which part to blame.

Konihaus is built the opposite way. Think of the classic Swiss army knife: one tool, many functions, everything in its place. Now picture a clean distributor with an endless number of sockets. Whatever you need today, you plug in. Whatever you need tomorrow, you add. Nothing gets stacked, nothing gets tangled, and nothing has to be replaced to make room.

That is how we think about a smart home:

Easy to extend. New lights, shades, sensors, or heating components join the existing system without starting over.
Easy to understand. You should be able to see what is connected and how it works, without needing a manual or a specialist.
One home, one system. Not ten apps and ten accounts, but a single place where everything comes together.

Quality Means Staying Power
In Switzerland, quality is not only about how something looks on the day it is delivered. It is about taking responsibility for it afterwards.
A smart home should work for many years. That means careful selection of devices, clean configuration, regular maintenance, and a service that is still there when something needs attention. It also means thinking about sustainability: a system that can grow and be repaired lasts longer than one that has to be replaced.

Rooted in Switzerland
The flag in our logo stands for a commitment: Konihaus is established in Switzerland, maintained in Switzerland, and stays in Switzerland.
This also applies to your data. Our local-first approach keeps your home's information on hardware in your home, and we do not move it permanently out of the country. (You can read more about this in our post on privacy by default.)

t: Who Is Konihaus For? Four Homes, One Principle
e: A retiree living alone, a renter who can't drill, a holiday-home owner far away, and an ordinary family home. Four situations, one approach - personal, local, private.
b:
"Is This Even for Someone Like Me?"
Smart home advertising usually shows the same picture: a young, tech-loving person with a tablet, in a brand-new flat. Most of the people I talk to look nothing like that. They are curious, but they are unsure whether any of this is meant for them.
So here is the honest answer. Konihaus is for four kinds of homes, and the same principle applies to all of them: personal, local, private.
The people below are illustrative examples, not real customers. They are composites of situations I expect to meet in the neighbourhood.

Seniors: Safety at Night, Independence by Day

The situation. Werner, 81, lives alone. He wants to stay in his own flat for as long as possible. His grandson worries, especially about the night, when a walk to the bathroom in the dark is the riskiest moment.
What we would set up.

Lights that come on softly when he gets out of bed, so he never has to find a switch
A quiet check-in: if there has been no movement by mid-morning, his grandson gets a message
A button by the bed that sends an alert to family

What matters. Werner does not have to wear anything or learn an app. The home simply looks after him a little. His grandson can stop worrying about every single night.
What it is not. It is not an emergency service and not a medical device, and I do not promise that nothing will happen. It is a set of small helpers that make an ordinary day and night a bit safer, and it supplements, never replaces, proper emergency arrangements.

Renters: Smart Without Drilling

The situation. Julia, 31, rents a flat in Zurich. The landlord allows no changes, the flat heats up in summer, and she is away for a week or two every month.
What we would set up.

Adhesive or plug-in devices: no drilling, no damage, nothing the landlord can object to
A smart plug that runs a fan when it gets too warm
Lights that vary a little while she is away
Sensors that tell her whether windows and doors are closed before she leaves

What matters. When she moves, the whole system moves with her. You take it down and put it up again in the next flat, and the flat looks the way it did before.

Holiday-Home Owners: Present Without Being There

The situation. Inge owns a holiday flat in Interlaken but now works near Zurich. Guests lock themselves out, heating runs in winter although nobody is there, and she only learns about a leak when the next guest arrives.
What we would set up.

A smart lock with one-time codes for guests, so no key

t: Your Home, Your Data: Privacy by Default
e: How Konihaus keeps smart-home data local, limits dependence on vendor clouds, and gives you control over remote access and connected services.
b:
Smart Home Privacy: Your Data Stays at Home
Google Home and Amazon Alexa are only the most obvious examples. A typical smart home may also include Philips Hue or IKEA lights, tado° thermostats, Somfy shades, Tuya devices, and products from several other manufacturers. Each ecosystem comes with its own app and account. Some apps are simple; others offer polished dashboards, themes, routines, and a long list of functions.
That convenience can come with a less visible cost: more vendor clouds, more external accounts, and more information about your home being processed outside it. With cloud-based voice assistants, commands, routines, and preferences are sent to remote servers. Other products differ in how much they can do locally, but many still rely on a manufacturer’s service for setup, control, notifications, or advanced features. You are not only choosing functions. You are also choosing who your home depends on and where its data may go.

Konihaus takes a local-first approach. Automations, device coordination, and the history needed to run your home are processed on hardware in your home. We select and configure devices for local communication wherever possible and clearly identify any optional feature that requires an external service. Your smart home does not need to report every action to a remote server simply to switch on a light, lower a shade, or adjust the heating.
How It Works
Your Konihaus system runs on a Home Assistant instance (a lightweight Linux computer, typically a Raspberry Pi or small NUC) installed in your home. All the logic—automations, device coordination, scenes—lives there.

Local-first data flow:

Your Zigbee devices talk directly to the local hub
Z-Wave devices stay local
WiFi devices communicate locally when supported
Konihaus does not collect your behavioral data

If you choose a device or service that requires its manufacturer’s cloud, that connection is treated as an explicit exception rather than the foundation of the system.
What This Means Practically
No data harvesting. Konihaus has no incentive to collect behavioral data. We don't monetize your attention or sell insights about your living patterns.
Less dependence on external services. Core automations continue to run at home, even if an internet service is unavailable. Cloud-dependent optional features remain subject to their provider.

Less lock-in. You can access your own data directly. Konihaus brings devices from established standards and ecosystems—such as Zigbe

t: Smart Home, Human Support
e: Smart home advice usually ends at the checkout. Personal service means one person stays with you afterwards.
b:
Good Advice Is Hard to Find
Ask around about smart home advice and you will notice a pattern. Independent, personal guidance is either hard to find or expensive. Most households end up piecing it together from product pages, forums and video tutorials.
That is odd, because the technology itself is rarely the hard part. The hard part is that nobody is responsible for the whole picture.
Advice That Ends at the Checkout
A visit to a large furniture or electronics store can be a fine start. Staff will often explain a product, and with some luck you leave with a useful tip. But once the product is paid for, you are mostly on your own with the manual. Where installation or support is offered at all, it is typically a paid extra, and it covers only that one manufacturer's products.
That is not a criticism of the people behind the counter. It is simply where their job ends.

Every Trade Adds Its Own Piece
Then there are the specialists who bring "smart" along with their own work:

The company that installs your shades offers a remote control, and calls it smart.
The company that fits your roof window offers its own motor and its own app.
The electrician installs everything from smart doorbells to lighting.
The plumber may screw smart thermostats onto your radiators, if that is part of the job at all.

Each of them does their part well. But each part comes with its own app, its own logic and its own limits, and none of them is responsible for making the pieces work together. When something does not, everyone points at the next trade.
The Real Cost Is Frustration
For someone who is not a technology enthusiast, this is exhausting. One app, then another. A device that works on Monday and not on Thursday. Nobody to ask. It is easy to lose motivation, and the attitude becomes: make it work, or forget about it.
Half-finished setups end up in a drawer, and the promise of a smarter home turns into one more chore.
It Does Not Have to Be Like That
A smart home is not supposed to be rocket science. Configuring and maintaining one properly is a craft, but for someone who does it regularly, it does not take much effort. Curious people can understand the basics quickly, and over time many do more and more on their own.
Even so, there is real convenience in having someone who guides you, and who is there when something unexpected happens. That is what personal service means: not doing everything for you forever, but staying beside you while you need it.

t: No Vendor Lock-In
e: Combine devices from different manufacturers without handing your entire smart home to a single ecosystem.
b:
What Vendor Lock-In Actually Means
Imagine a home with Philips Hue lights, a Sonos speaker system, tado° thermostats, and a few Sonoff or Shelly sensors. Outside, there may be an Intex spa, a Worx Landroid robotic mower, and a Netatmo weather station. Each product may work well on its own. Each also tends to arrive with its own app, account, terminology, and way of creating schedules or scenes.
The difficulty becomes clear when you want them to act as one home. You may want the shades to close, the lights to dim, and the music to start when the living room becomes too warm. You may want the mower to pause when the weather station detects rain, or receive one meaningful alert instead of checking five separate apps. The individual products can be smart while the overall home remains fragmented.

Apple Home and Google Home can bring many compatible products into one interface, and standards such as Matter are improving the situation. They do not remove every boundary, however. Support still depends on the precise model, generation, bridge, manufacturer account, region, and functions exposed by the integration. A product may appear in the shared app while some of its settings remain available only in the manufacturer's own app.
Now imagine that you find Paulmann smart lights that suit a room better than your existing bulbs, or you decide to replace several mixed sensors with Sonoff models. In a tightly controlled ecosystem, that apparently simple purchase can lead to a new bridge, another account, rebuilt scenes, or the loss of functions you already use. The old hardware does not literally become worthless, but the time invested in connecting and automating it may not transfer cleanly.
That is vendor lock-in: changing one part of the system carries consequences far beyond that device.
Konihaus Connects Different Systems
Konihaus uses Home Assistant as a common automation layer. It can bring together devices and services that communicate through Zigbee, Z-Wave, Matter, WiFi, MQTT, local network interfaces, and supported manufacturer integrations. Instead of asking every product to understand every other product, the central system translates their states and controls into one consistent model.

This does not mean that every smart device is automatically compatible or fully local. Some products expose only part of their functionality. Others still require a manufacturer account or cloud connection. Compatibility can also change between product generations; tado°

t: Smart Home Is Today's Fine Dining
e: Obsession or pointless? With smart homes, the truth is in the middle.
k: is a smart home worth it
b:
There is a certain kind of person who can talk for an hour about wine. The soil, the vintage, the one bottle that changed everything. And there is a certain kind of person who can do the same about their smart home: the Zigbee mesh, the automation that finally works, the sensor that caught a leak at 3 a.m.
I've noticed that the smart home today feels a lot like fine dining.

Two reactions, both fair
For some people, it's simply too much. Too complex, too fiddly, maybe even a little dangerous, and certainly expensive. Just like a tasting menu with wine pairing, it looks like something for people with time, money and a particular passion.
For others, it's pointless. Whatever can break will break, and a light switch has worked fine for a hundred years. Why add a layer of software to something that already works?
Both reactions are reasonable. Both are also, I think, incomplete.

The enthusiasts are not the whole story
Every field has its obsessives, and they matter: they push things forward, find the rough edges and make the rest of us curious. But a hobby for a few is not the same as value for many.
Think about how good food and wine reached more people. Not because everyone became a sommelier. Restaurants got more approachable, quality became easier to find, and you no longer needed to know everything to enjoy a good meal. Expertise moved from the diner's side to the kitchen's side.
The smart home is at the same point. It becomes useful for most people when they no longer have to be the expert.

Remember the phone
Before 2007, the smartphone wasn't a mass-market idea. Today almost everyone in the Western world has one.
I'm not claiming the smart home will have its "iPhone moment". Let's be honest: it isn't as sexy. Nobody queues overnight for a motion sensor. Products alone won't create this demand.
But meaningful automations and understandable insights from our homes can. We already accept this from our cars, which tell us when something needs attention and how efficiently we drive. Our homes are just as worthy of that kind of clarity.

What it is really about
Don't get me wrong: the coffee won't brew itself. (Well, sometimes it might. :)) But that was never the goal.
The goal is to make things better:

Remove small, recurring annoyances, like the light left on, the door you're not sure you locked, the window open in winter.
Stop overspending on heating, standby power and things we would never choose to pay for if we saw them.

t: Will It Still Work in Ten Years?
e: A smart home does not have to age like a gadget. The platform keeps developing, and your system grows with new standards.
b:
"Won't This Be Obsolete in Two Years?"
Anyone who has bought a phone, a TV or a laptop knows the feeling: a year or two later, it is already yesterday's model. So when someone offers to build a smart system into your home, the hesitation is completely reasonable. Nobody wants to invest in something that ends up in a drawer.
The fear is fair. But it helps to ask a more precise question: what actually makes a smart home age badly?
What Really Makes a Smart Home Age
Rarely the hardware. Lights, sensors and switches tend to last for years. What ages badly is dependence on one company.
In 2016, Nest, owned by Alphabet, permanently switched off all Revolv hubs. In 2022, the smart home company Insteon shut down abruptly, leaving customers without the service their system relied on. In both cases, the devices did not wear out. The company behind them stopped, and with it, the parts of the system that lived on its servers.
That is the real obsolescence risk: not the age of your devices, but whether your home depends on someone else's business decisions.
Think Kitchen, Not Gadget
A good kitchen is not replaced when the oven breaks. You replace the oven. The sockets, the wiring and the layout stay, and a new appliance simply plugs in.
A smart home can work the same way. It has three layers:

Standards are the sockets. Open standards such as Zigbee, Z-Wave and Matter mean that devices from many makers speak the same language, and they outlive individual brands.
Devices are the appliances. A sensor, a lamp or a thermostat can be replaced one at a time, when it breaks or when something better comes along.
The brain is the software that connects everything and decides what happens. It runs in your home and is updated over time.

When these layers are separate, nothing forces you to start over. One part changes, and the rest keeps working.

A Brain That Keeps Learning
The software at the centre of a Konihaus system is Home Assistant, which is developed openly and updated regularly. When a new standard arrives, support for it is added to the software, and your system learns it without being replaced. Matter is a good example: Konihaus runs Matter devices locally, without needing an internet connection or cloud services.
"For free" needs one honest note: the software updates cost nothing, and they are part of the service. New devices are a separate decision, and you only buy them if you want them. The point is that you never have to.

t: Warm When You Arrive, Quiet When You Leave
e: Automatic heating and shading only help if they actually run — without anyone remembering.
k: save energy with a smart home
b:
The Savings Everyone Knows About, and Rarely Gets
Turn the heating down when nobody's home. Close the shades before the afternoon sun hits. Switch off the standby power nobody uses. None of this is a secret. It's the kind of advice that appears in every energy-saving checklist, every utility newsletter, every well-meaning article.
The problem was never knowing what to do. It's that doing it reliably, every day, for years, without becoming a chore, is a different matter entirely. A thermostat you have to remember to adjust gets adjusted for a week and then forgotten. A shade you have to close by hand stays open on the one afternoon you're not there to close it.

Where This Becomes a Real Problem: The Holiday Home
The gap between knowing and doing is easy to underestimate at home. It becomes obvious the moment the property is somewhere you're not.
A holiday home often runs one of two ways: a caretaker or property company visits occasionally and handles the essentials, energy efficiency included, if it hasn't slipped down the list that week. Or nobody visits at all between stays, and the heating either runs at full temperature the whole time, burning money for no reason, or gets switched off completely, risking cold-related damage and a very unpleasant first evening back.
Automation removes the guesswork from both sides. Heating can hold a low, safe baseline temperature while the house is empty, and be raised to a comfortable level a few hours before you arrive, so the property is warm by the time you walk in rather than heating up around you. The same logic runs in reverse when you leave.

Shading and Ventilation Do Quiet, Constant Work
Heating and cooling get the attention, but shades and ventilation carry a surprising share of the load. In summer, shades that close automatically before direct sun hits a south-facing window keep a room from heating up in the first place, which is a cheaper problem to solve than cooling it back down afterward.
Ventilation matters just as much, particularly in a property that stands empty for stretches at a time. Controlled air exchange keeps humidity from building up in closed rooms, which is one of the more common ways mold gets started in an unoccupied home. A scheduled or humidity-triggered ventilation cycle addresses this without anyone having to think about it.

Moving the Expensive Hours
